newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Trade in Asian currencies set to soar further.
newsitem.headline: Trade in Asian currencies set to soar further.

text.p: Trade in exotic Asian currencies is set to surge further in the next 12-18 months, despite a possible fall in the inflows of short-term capital seeking high interest rates, economists said on Tuesday.
They said yield play, which dominated much of this year's activity, could dwindle next year as the prospect of lower interest rates in Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand loomed.
But regional currencies would continue to be actively traded on the back of growing intra-regional trade and the increased de-regulation of Asia's financial markets.

Average daily volume in Asian regional currencies in the spot market totalled US$26.03 billion in 1995, according to a survey in the Singapore Foreign Exchange Market Committee (SFEMC)'s recently released 1996 annual report.

The report said swap and forward markets saw average daily turnover of US$22.60 billion in the currencies of 10 Asian economies surveyed: Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Philippines, China, Hong Kong, Taiwan, South Korea and India.
The Thai baht had the highest average daily turnover with US$5 billion on the spot and US$9 billion on the forward market.
The SFEMC said the growth of Asian currency markets had been aligned to trade and investment flows in the region as most Asian monetary authorities discouraged speculative activity.
It said trade flows would increase with further economic liberalisation, leading to higher trading volumes in regional currencies and a greater availability of hedging instruments.
Desmond Supple, senior emerging markets economist at research firm I.D.E.A. said the current market size for trading Asian currencies was still far below its potential.

"Trade on the Asian exotics accounts for only around 3-4 percent of total turnover on the global forex market. But in terms of merchandise trade, Asia excluding Japan, accounts for around 20 percent of world trade," Supple said.
He said the long-term trend for trade growth in Asia was intact despite a recent downturn in the exports of some countries, due partly to a decline in global electronics demand.

The creation of a single European currency would also divert increased trading interest to Asia, reinforcing a recent trend among banks to beef up their regional currency desks in Singapore, he added.

Kobus van der Wath, regional head of treasury economics at Standard Chartered Bank said the prospect of lower interest rates in some Asian countries next year would not significantly deter investors as yields in the region remained high relative to Europe, the United States and Japan.
He said the growth of Asian equity and debt markets would also trigger increased demand for their currencies.

The SFEMC report said Asian bond markets were still at an early stage of development but huge demand for funds for a number of infrastructure projects and the corporatisation of state enterprises would lead to increased bond issues.

The combined size of the 10 countries' bond markets was US$453 billion, or 21 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) at the end of 1994. This compared with the U.S. bond market which stood at US$7,429 billion, or 110 percent of GDP.

The report said notwithstanding the conservative fiscal policies of Asian governments, private sector demand was expected to propel the Asian bond market to an estimated US$686 billion, or 25 percent of GDP in 1996.
